KEY MESSAGE 1...Any lingering showers exit the Cape and Islands by late
morning, giving way to a dry afternoon and evening. Fall-like 
temperatures expected Saturday with dry conditions. 

The remaining batch of showers continues to push east early this 
morning. Any remaining showers will likely exit the Cape and Islands 
by late morning. Behind the showers, a cold front moves across the 
region early this morning shifting winds to the NW. High pressure 
will settle across the region for today with subsident flow 
supporting dry conditions and clearing skies. NW winds with some 
gusts to 20 and up to 25 mph for the Cape/Islands. Cooler air begins 
to advect in from the north in the mid-levels later today, but 
likely won't have much impact on the high temperatures. Temperatures 
are likely to be in seasonable ranges in the 70s for most areas. 
Only exceptions may be upper 60s for the outer Cape and Nantucket 
where there is northerly onshore flow.

A cooler airmass pushes into the region later Friday into Saturday. 
Clear skies will optimize radiational cooling as well to make for a 
cool night. Temperatures likely fall into the upper 40s to low 50s 
for much of the region. Higher elevations, especially the northern 
Worcester Hills will lean cooler in the low 40s. Cooler airmass 
stays in place for Saturday with 850mb temperatures 6-9C. This will 
support Fall-like temperatures in the mid 60s for most. 
East/northeast flow along the eastern coastline may keep those 
immediate coastal areas cooler in the low 60s. Surface high pressure 
continues to dominate bringing dry conditions. 

Not exactly ideal beach weather with the cooler temperatures; 
however, there is an increased risk for rip currents for the east-
facing beaches. There will be an extended period of enhanced NNE 
winds tonight into Saturday which will help establish a swell with 
slightly longer wave periods. 


KEY MESSAGE 2...Next chance for rain Sunday into Monday. There 
remains uncertainty in the details such as coverage, timing, and
amounts. Showers may linger through early next week. 

The main surface high exits offshore Saturday night into early 
Sunday as the next system approaches from the west with our next 
chance of precipitation Sunday into Monday. The ingredients are 
generally in place for at at least a soaking rainfall across 
southern New England. A shortwave approaches from the northwest 
coupled with an 850mb jet positioning over southern New England. 
This provide ample moisture advecting and synoptic scale lift for 
precipitation. PWATS increase to 1.0-1.8" (150-180 percent of 
normal), which is anomalous compared to climo. A low pressure system 
tracks east from the Great Lakes region Sunday putting southern New 
England in the warm sector as its warm front shifts northward. With 
the ample moisture and additional forcing this raises some flags for 
heavy rain potential or at least embedded heavy showers.

There is still variance across guidance in the exact track of 
the system/low pressure which has resulted in lower confidence 
in the details such as timing, amounts, and the potential for 
heavy rain. There has also been lacking consistency run to run 
within individual guidance as well. There is at least a general 
consensus across guidance that the higher moisture and better 
forcing(warm front) will more likely be south. This would favor 
our more south, southwest areas for higher rain totals. GFS and 
Canadian solutions (deterministic & ensemble) seem to reflect 
that pattern with higher amounts south while the ECMWF has a 
wider footprint with generally higher totals. When it comes to 
amounts solutions vary from 0.30" to 1.0" across ensembles based
on the 25-50th percentiles. Deterministic guidance had 
displayed more "aggressive" solutions with swaths of higher 
amounts >1.0". However, these solutions have had the most 
variance from run to run which further adds to the uncertainty. 
The most likely case at this point will be anywhere from a few 
tenths to an inch. This seems reasonable given the mean track. 
There isn't much indication of instability which should limit 
the heavier rain rates. If the warm frontal forcing shifts north
enough, we could get embedded heavy rain supporting by the 
added lift and efficient rain processes. So overall, there is 
confidence that we will get at least a soaking rain with rain 
arriving through the day Sunday continuing into Monday. We'll 
need to continue monitoring for the isolated heavy rain 
potential as models come into better agreement with the track 
over the next day or so. 

It is also possible showers may linger across the south coast and 
Cape and Islands Monday into Tuesday. This will depend on if the low 
or a boundary stalls across the waters. Wednesday leans mainly dry 
with potential for another system to arrive late-week with rain 
possible.
